strengths: Understanding why distributional RL improves learning is an important research question. The fitted-iteration perspective provides a useful framework for discussing loss geometry, optimization, and representation.

Applying Sinkhorn losses to particle-based return estimates is a plausible algorithmic direction. Results across ten Atari games show preliminary competitiveness, including encouraging performance on SpaceInvaders.

The manuscript cites relevant foundational work, supplies proof appendices and several implementation hyperparameters, and explicitly acknowledges limitations concerning exploration and contraction at finite regularization.
weaknesses: The foundational decomposition in Eq. 4 is invalid for general return distributions, including the absolutely continuous distributions assumed earlier. Writing P = (1−ε)δ_E[Z] + εµ with 0<ε<1 requires positive probability mass at the mean. For a uniform distribution on [−1,1], the proposed residual instead has µ({0}) = −(1−ε)/ε, so µ is not a probability distribution. Algebraic subtraction does not guarantee a valid distribution. Consequently, the claimed entropy-regularized interpretation and results relying on this probabilistic decomposition lack their stated foundation.

Theorem 4 is incorrect as written. With its specified cost c(x,y)=−|x−y|², point masses at 0 and 1 give the debiased loss −2 for every regularization strength, contradicting the claimed positive Wasserstein limit. Correcting the sign still requires distinguishing Wα from Wα^α and MMD from squared MMD; the asserted range of all real α is also unjustified. These issues leave both the theorem and the implemented loss unclear.

The maximum-entropy connection is not established by Theorem 1. Appendix D introduces a new cross-entropy-augmented reward and invokes ordinary policy-evaluation convergence. It does not show that neural Z-fitting implements this modified Bellman operator or maximizes the proposed objective. Moreover, treating the augmented reward and policy as fixed requires justification when both depend on the learned parameters.

The stability analysis supports a substantially narrower conclusion than advertised. Theorem 2 applies standard convex SGD stability arguments to a softmax model with fixed bounded features and fixed targets. It does not establish generalization for jointly learned neural representations and evolving RL data. The same softmax smoothness holds with hard targets, while squared loss with fixed bounded features is also smooth. Thus, these properties do not establish an intrinsic advantage of learning the full return distribution.

The acceleration theorem is not proved as stated. Theorem 3 specifies ε=1/(1+τ), whereas Appendix I uses ε=1/(1+κ). Its O(κ) upper bound cannot establish the claimed nonconvergence when κ is large. The accelerated regime additionally assumes gradient noise decreases with the requested accuracy, without deriving this condition from distributional approximation or testing it experimentally. This does not substantiate the claimed explanation of sample-efficiency differences across games.

Experimental support and reproducibility are insufficient for the performance claims. The ten-game study provides no reported seed counts, defined uncertainty estimates, aggregate normalized comparison, or sufficiently specified evaluation protocol. No implementation is supplied or linked, and referencing existing MMD implementations does not resolve the loss ambiguity. IQN and FQF are discussed but not evaluated, and computational overhead from Sinkhorn iterations is unreported. The single-game t-SNE visualization also cannot establish tighter clusters in the original representation space or correctness of the predicted action classes.

The remaining algorithmic novelty is limited to applying established Sinkhorn machinery to an existing particle representation. The KL/histogram analysis is not connected to optimization of the proposed finite-regularization Sinkhorn algorithm, and the high-dimensional sample-complexity motivation does not directly apply to scalar returns. The preliminary empirical results do not compensate for the fundamental failures in the central theoretical contributions; these technical issues determine the strong-reject recommendation.
